questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old patient presents to the outpatient clinic 4 weeks following an acute myocardial infarction with low-grade fever, pleuritic chest pain that eases when leaning forward, and an elevated ESR. Dressler's syndrome is suspected. When does this condition typically occur?
questions.explanation: Dressler's (post-cardiac injury) syndrome: autoimmune pericarditis 2-10 weeks post-MI or cardiac surgery. Fever, pleuritis, pericardial effusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: An emergency department physician reviews an ECG that shows prominent Osborne (J) waves. This pathognomonic finding is most classically associated with which condition?
questions.explanation: Osborne/J waves: positive deflection at J-point, pathognomonic of hypothermia. Also seen in hypercalcemia but hypothermia is classic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A post-mortem myocardial tissue biopsy reveals microscopic granulomatous structures containing specialized Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells. These Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic for which condition?
questions.explanation: Aschoff bodies (granulomas with Anitschkow cells/caterpillar cells) are pathognomonic of rheumatic fever, seen in myocardium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A patient presenting with an acute myocardial infarction is noted to have frank pulmonary edema on clinical examination. According to the Killip classification system for heart failure in acute MI, which class does this represent?
questions.explanation: Killip classification: I=no failure, II=S3 + basal crackles, III=frank pulmonary edema, IV=cardiogenic shock. Mortality increases with class.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old male with end-stage renal disease presents with severe weakness. An emergency ECG demonstrates tall, peaked T waves along with widening of the QRS complexes. Which electrolyte imbalance is responsible for this sequence?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia sequence: peaked T → flat P → wide QRS → sine wave → VF. Treatment: calcium gluconate first (membrane stabilization).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old male with a family history of sudden cardiac death undergoes an ECG screen. The tracing reveals a characteristic coved-type ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads. In Brugada syndrome, this hallmark ECG change is localized to which leads?
questions.explanation: Brugada: coved-type ST elevation in V1-V2 (Type 1 pattern). Causes sudden death due to VF. SCN5A mutation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with acute palpitations. His blood pressure is stable at 122/78 mmHg. The ECG reveals an irregularly irregular rhythm with an absent P-wave axis. What is the most appropriate initial management choice?
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation: rate control is first-line unless hemodynamically unstable. Beta-blockers (metoprolol) or calcium channel blockers are used.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: Which electrocardiographic manifestation is considered the most specific diagnostic feature for a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome during sinus rhythm?

options.B: Short PR interval with a delta wave

questions.explanation: WPW: short PR <120ms + delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) due to accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female experiences episodic paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). During an acute episode in the clinic, vagal maneuvers fail. Which short-acting drug is the first line choice for termination?
questions.explanation: Adenosine is DOC for termination of PSVT/SVT. It transiently blocks AV node. Very short half-life (~10 sec).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old patient with known Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome develops rapid atrial fibrillation. Which of the following antiarrhythmic drugs is considered safe to administer?
questions.explanation: WPW + AF: drugs blocking AV node (digoxin, verapamil, adenosine) are CONTRAINDICATED — may increase conduction through accessory pathway. Procainamide/DC cardioversion are safe.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 54-year-old patient presents with acute, crushing substernal chest pain. The diagnostic ECG shows clear ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
questions.explanation: Inferior MI (II, III, aVF) = RCA territory (85% cases). Check RV leads (V3R, V4R) for right ventricular MI.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A stable 65-year-old patient presents with a regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia at a rate of 180 bpm. Which pharmacological agent is the most appropriate first-line choice?
questions.explanation: Stable wide-complex tachycardia (likely VT): amiodarone is first-line. Verapamil is CONTRAINDICATED in VT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: An 18-year-old competitive runner collapses suddenly during a track meet. Post-mortem analysis shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy. What is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes?
questions.explanation: HOCM (HCM) is the most common cause of sudden death in young athletes in the USA. Pathognomonic: asymmetric septal hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, EF < 40%) develops rapid atrial fibrillation. Which class of drugs is preferred first-line for long-term ventricular rate control?
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers (carvedilol/metoprolol) are preferred in AF with HFrEF. Digoxin can be added but not first-line alone.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A physician is reviewing antiarrhythmic therapy for a patient. Which of the following drugs significantly prolongs the QT interval, requiring close monitoring, even though it paradoxically has a low risk of inducing Torsades de Pointes?
questions.explanation: Amiodarone prolongs QT but paradoxically rarely causes TdP. However, it is listed as a QT-prolonging drug. Other drugs: quinidine, sotalol, haloperidol, macrolides.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 56-year-old male presents with severe chest pain. ECG shows ST-segment elevations in leads V1 through V4. Which coronary artery branch is acutely occluded?
questions.explanation: ST elevations in leads V1-V4 represent an anterior/anteroseptal wall myocardial infarction, which corresponds to the territory supplied by the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) coronary artery.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male with uncontrolled hypertension presents with sudden-onset, catastrophic 'tearing' chest pain radiating to his back. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg, and his heart rate is 105 bpm. A CT angiogram confirms an acute Stanford Type A aortic dissection. What is the most critical immediate pharmacological target before emergency surgical intervention?

options.A: Aggressive IV fluid volume resuscitation to combat impending shock
options.B: Rapid heart rate and shear-stress control with IV beta-blockers (e.g., esmolol) to a target HR < 60 bpm
options.C: Immediate systemic anticoagulation with a bolus of unfractionated heparin
options.D: Monotherapy with high-dose IV nitroprusside to rapidly reduce systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg

questions.explanation: In acute aortic dissection, the primary medical management objective is to reduce the shear stress on the aortic wall. Intravenous beta-blockers (such as esmolol or labetalol) must be given first to lower the heart rate below 60 bpm. Vasodilators like nitroprusside should never be given alone or first, as they can cause reflex tachycardia, worsening the tearing forces.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 74-year-old male presents with dyspnea on exertion, angina, and an operational history of exertional syncope. On cardiac auscultation, there is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard loudest at the right upper sternal border that radiates to his carotids, alongside a delayed carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus). What is the definitive management for this severe structural defect?

options.A: Long-term conservative medical titration using high-dose loop diuretics and beta-blockers
options.B: Surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (SAVR/TAVR)
options.D: Empiric continuous intravenous infusion of positive inotropes

questions.explanation: The clinical triad of dyspnea, angina, and syncope combined with a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur and pulsus parvus et tardus indicates critical, symptomatic aortic stenosis. Once symptoms manifest, survival drops precipitously, and definitive mechanical intervention via surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (SAVR/TAVR) is indicated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 34-year-old female with a history of intravenous drug use presents with a persistent fever, chills, and a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Physical examination reveals painless erythematous macules on her palms and soles. Which of the following correctly pairs her peripheral sign with the expected causative organism?
questions.explanation: The patient has acute infective endocarditis secondary to IV drug use, typically affecting the tricuspid valve (indicated by a holosystolic murmur increasing with inspiration—Carvallo's sign). The painless erythematous macules on the palms/soles are Janeway lesions, caused by septic emboli, which are highly characteristic of acute endocarditis driven by Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female with metastatic breast cancer presents to the emergency department with profound dyspnea, tachycardia, and distant, muffled heart sounds. Her blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg, and she exhibits a drop in systolic blood pressure of 14 mmHg during inspiration. Jugular venous distension is present. What is the immediate life-saving procedure required?

options.A: Emergent electrical synchronized cardioversion at 100 J
options.B: Intravenous administration of high-dose bolus furosemide
options.D: Urgent structural surgical patch repair of the ventricular wall

questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with Beck's triad (hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds) along with an exaggerated pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop in systolic pressure during inspiration), diagnostic of cardiac tamponade. In the setting of hemodynamic instability, an emergent subxiphoid pericardiocentesis is required to decompress the pericardial space.
